title: LRU and LFU Cache
tagline: O(1) get and put with smart eviction — LRU via hashmap + doubly linked list, LFU adding a frequency layer.

sections.content:
A **cache** is a fixed-capacity store that keeps the most valuable data close for fast retrieval, discarding old data to make room for new. The challenging part is the **eviction policy** — which item to remove when the cache is full. Two policies dominate real-world systems:

**LRU (Least Recently Used)** evicts the item that has gone the longest without being accessed. The intuition is temporal locality: if you haven't touched something recently, you probably won't need it soon. LRU is the default cache policy for CPU memory caches, OS page replacement, database buffer pools, and web caches.

**LFU (Least Frequently Used)** evicts the item that has been accessed the fewest total times. It is a better model for workloads with stable hot-spot access patterns — frequently accessed items stay forever. The cost is more complex bookkeeping.

Both policies require **O(1) get and O(1) put** to be practical. Achieving O(1) for LRU requires combining a **hash map** (O(1) key lookup) with a **doubly linked list** (O(1) reordering). LFU adds a second layer of frequency tracking.

sections.title: A Whiteboard and a Sticky-Note Stack
sections.content:
Imagine you have a whiteboard with space for only 5 sticky notes. Every time you look up a piece of information you move its sticky note to the **top** of the stack. When you need space for a new note you discard the one at the **bottom** — the note you haven't touched longest.

This is LRU. The hash map is the index on the side of the whiteboard that tells you where each note currently is. Moving a note to the top is O(1) because a doubly linked list lets you splice a node out and prepend it in constant time — no shifting, no scanning. Without the doubly linked list, moving a note to the top would require scanning the entire stack to find it — O(n). Without the hash map, finding the note for a given key would require scanning the list — also O(n). Together, the two data structures give O(1) for every operation.

**LRU Implementation** uses two structures in tandem:
1. A `Map<key, DLLNode>` for O(1) lookup by key.
2. A doubly linked list where the **head** is the most recently used (MRU) and the **tail** is the least recently used (LRU).

**get(key)**: look up the node in the map; if found, move it to the head (mark as most recently used) and return its value; otherwise return -1.

**put(key, value)**: if the key exists, update the node's value and move it to head. If not and capacity is full, delete the map entry for the tail node and remove the tail — then insert a new node at the head and add to the map.

Every operation — lookup, move-to-front, tail-remove, head-insert — is O(1) with a doubly linked list and hash map.

**LFU Implementation** adds a **frequency dimension**. Every node has a `frequency` counter. The LFU evicts the node with the lowest frequency; among ties, it evicts the least recently used (LRU within that frequency bucket). The canonical O(1) LFU uses:
- A `Map<key, {value, freq}>` for key lookup.
- A `Map<freq, LinkedHashSet<key>>` mapping each frequency to the ordered set of keys at that frequency — the LRU ordering within a bucket.
- A `minFreq` variable tracking the current minimum frequency.

**get(key)**: increment the key's frequency, move it from its old frequency bucket to the new one, update `minFreq` if needed.

**put(key, value)**: if at capacity, evict the LRU key from the `minFreq` bucket, then insert the new key at frequency 1 and set `minFreq = 1`.

LFU has higher implementation complexity and potentially worse performance for one-time-access items (a scan over a large dataset floods the cache with frequency-1 items). LRU is simpler and covers most real-world use cases.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Empty
  Empty --> Partial: put(key,val)\ncapacity not full
  Partial --> Partial: get(key)\nmove to MRU
  Partial --> Full: put until cap
  Full --> Full: get(key)\nmove to MRU
  Full --> Full: put(new key)\nevict LRU tail\ninsert at head
sections.caption: LRU cache state machine: get always moves the accessed node to MRU position; put on a full cache evicts the LRU tail before inserting the new node at the head.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Dummy head and tail sentinels eliminate null-checks in `#remove` and `#insertFront` — every node always has both neighbours. The Map stores direct node references, so get and put are truly O(1): one map lookup, two pointer adjustments.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: JavaScript's `Set` maintains insertion order and `values().next().value` retrieves the oldest key in O(1). This gives each frequency bucket the LRU ordering for tie-breaking. When `minFreq` bucket becomes empty after `#incrFreq`, incrementing `minFreq` is valid only when the trigger was a get/put-update — new insertions always reset `minFreq = 1`.

sections.content: **LRU is the single most common cache design question in system design interviews.** The key insight to state immediately: you need two data structures — a hash map for O(1) lookup and a doubly linked list for O(1) recency reordering. A singly linked list cannot splice in O(1). An array cannot reorder in O(1). JavaScript's `Map` iterates in insertion order, so `Map` alone can simulate LRU — evict `map.keys().next().value` (oldest entry) — but understanding the doubly-linked-list approach shows deeper systems knowledge.

items: LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the item untouched longest; LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts the item accessed fewest total times.
O(1) LRU requires a HashMap (O(1) key lookup) combined with a doubly linked list (O(1) move-to-front and tail removal) — neither structure alone achieves both.
Dummy head and tail sentinels simplify doubly linked list operations by eliminating null checks at the boundaries.
O(1) LFU requires three data structures: a key→{value,freq} map, a freq→Set(keys) map for bucketing, and a minFreq variable tracking which bucket to evict from.
LRU suits temporal-locality workloads (web caches, OS page tables, CPU caches); LFU suits stable hot-spot workloads but is harder to implement and can be polluted by one-time large scans.

quiz.question: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?
options: Doubly linked lists use less memory than singly linked lists
Removing a node from the middle of the list requires O(1) access to the previous node — impossible with a singly linked list without scanning
Doubly linked lists allow faster hash map lookups
Singly linked lists do not support head insertion
quiz.explanation: When a node is accessed (get) it must be moved to the head. Splicing a node out requires updating the previous node's next pointer and the next node's prev pointer — both available in O(1) in a doubly linked list. With a singly linked list, finding the previous node requires O(n) traversal.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of dummy head and tail sentinel nodes in an LRU implementation?
options: They store metadata about cache capacity and hit rate
They eliminate null-pointer checks — every real node always has both neighbours
They act as the MRU and LRU items respectively
They are required to make the HashMap work with the linked list
quiz.explanation: Without sentinels, insert-at-head and remove-from-tail must special-case empty lists (null.prev, null.next). With dummy nodes, every real node always has a non-null prev and next, so the pointer rewiring code is identical for all positions — simpler and less error-prone.

quiz.question: In an LRU cache of capacity 3 with operations: put(1), put(2), put(3), get(1), put(4). Which key is evicted?
quiz.explanation: After put(1,2,3) the order is [3,2,1] (3=MRU, 1=LRU). get(1) moves 1 to MRU: [1,3,2]. put(4) at capacity evicts the LRU tail: 2. Order becomes [4,1,3].

quiz.question: What three data structures are needed for an O(1) LFU cache?
options: Min-heap, hash map, and sorted array
key→{value,freq} map, freq→ordered-set-of-keys map, and a minFreq variable
Two doubly linked lists and a hash map
Priority queue, hash map, and doubly linked list
quiz.explanation: The key→{value,freq} map gives O(1) value and frequency lookup. The freq→ordered-set map groups keys by frequency and provides O(1) access to the oldest key in the minimum-frequency bucket. minFreq tracks which frequency bucket to evict from without scanning all buckets.

quiz.question: Why must minFreq be reset to 1 whenever a new key is inserted in an LFU cache?
options: New keys must always be evicted first
New keys always start with frequency 1, which is always the lowest possible frequency
Resetting minFreq prevents overflow of the frequency counter
JavaScript Sets do not support frequency tracking
quiz.explanation: A newly inserted key has frequency 1 — the minimum possible value. Even if an existing key has frequency 1, the new key was inserted more recently (LRU tie-breaking). Setting minFreq = 1 ensures the next eviction correctly targets the frequency-1 bucket.

quiz.question: Under what access pattern does LFU outperform LRU?
options: A sequential scan through a large dataset (each key accessed exactly once)
A stable hot-spot pattern where a small number of keys are accessed repeatedly over time
A random access pattern where every key is equally likely
A pattern where the most recently accessed key is always needed next
quiz.explanation: LFU protects frequently accessed keys from eviction even if they haven't been accessed very recently. In a stable hot-spot pattern (e.g. a popular product page hit thousands of times), LFU keeps it in cache indefinitely. LRU might evict it after a brief cold period.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of get and put in a properly implemented LRU cache using a HashMap and doubly linked list?
options: O(log n)
O(1) amortised
O(1) worst case
O(n) worst case for put when cache is full
quiz.explanation: Both operations are O(1) worst case: get does one Map lookup plus two pointer updates; put does one Map lookup, one Map insert/update, one node creation, and a constant number of pointer updates — all O(1). Eviction is also O(1) because the LRU node is always at the tail.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a real-world system that uses an LRU eviction policy?
options: A database transaction log — uses FIFO, not LRU
Redis with maxmemory-policy=allkeys-lru — evicts least recently accessed keys
A Bloom filter — uses probabilistic membership, not eviction
A Union-Find structure — does not cache data
quiz.explanation: Redis supports several eviction policies including allkeys-lru (evict any key by LRU) and volatile-lru (evict keys with TTL by LRU). This is configured via maxmemory-policy and is one of the most common LRU applications in backend engineering.

quiz.question: What is the 'cache pollution' problem that can affect LFU more than LRU?
options: Hash collisions that slow down lookups in the frequency map
A large one-time scan that fills the cache with frequency-1 items, blocking new hot items from entering
Concurrent writes that corrupt frequency counters in multi-threaded environments
The minFreq variable going out of sync with actual frequencies
quiz.explanation: LFU keeps keys based on total access count. A sequential full-table scan — where every record is accessed exactly once — fills the LFU cache with frequency-1 items. These items then compete with genuinely hot items on an equal footing, displacing them. LRU handles this better because scan items are immediately marked 'least recently used' after access.

quiz.question: In JavaScript, can a plain `Map` simulate a basic LRU cache without a custom doubly linked list?
options: No — JavaScript Map has no ordering guarantee
Yes — JavaScript Map iterates in insertion order, so the first key returned by map.keys() is always the oldest (LRU)
Yes — but only for caches with capacity less than 100
No — Map operations are O(n), making it unsuitable for caches
quiz.explanation: JavaScript's Map is specified to iterate in insertion order. For LRU, you can delete-and-re-insert a key on access (promoting it to newest), and evict via `map.keys().next().value` (the oldest key). This gives a clean LRU implementation without a custom linked list — though it has slightly higher constant factors than the DLL approach.
